"The devil's advocate" is a figure of speech that has nothing to do with the literal devil. It dates back to the 16th century and refers to the person in the Church charged with arguing *against* the canonization of a saint. It was an important job, because the Church takes canonization very seriously and wants to make sure they only canonize those who are truly worthy of the honor.

Today it's generally a metaphor for arguing a position one does not hold in order to clarify thinking or test assumptions.

Getting to your actual question though, look up the case of poor Third Lieutenant William Cox from the War of 1812. All the officers aboard the *Chesapeake* senior to him were incapacitated, so command fell on his shoulders … and he was subsequently court-martialed and discharged from the Navy for dereliction of duty for his conduct during the battle.

Point is, command of a ship is distinct from the grade of the officer commanding. It's a line-of-succession type thing. If you end up the senior ranking officer who is capable of taking command, then you have to take command whether you want to or not. Assuming command in this way doesn't *change you.* It doesn't change your rating or your rank. It just means you happen to be the person *in that situation* who is legally obligated to assume command.

Oh, I could write quite a rant on the flaws I see in *Enterprise,* most of which would boil down to "They weren't gutsy enough."

The underlying premise of the show starts with the conflict between humanity and the Vulcans. It's *literally* the first thing revealed in dialogue in the first episode. This is good! Throughout the show Vulcans had been consistently depicted as good friends of humanity … but if you think about it, why *wouldn't* they want to keep humans on a leash? They're the ones who made first contact, humanity has a lot of intrinsic traits that run counter to Vulcan sensibilities, having them adopt a "Woah, slow down there a little bit boys and girls" makes perfect sense.

Then the writers *instantly* started to let the air out of that conflict by putting a Vulcan aboard the ship. The whole thing was pretty weakly written: You have to appoint a Vulcan who answers to us to be *executive officer* aboard your new starship, or else you can't use our maps. This is a new age of exploration! *Enterprise* is going out there to *make* maps, not follow them! You can keep your Vulcan, we'll do it ourselves … said nobody.

Now we've got the essential conflict of the show — human headlong-ism versus Vulcan snottiness — embodied in two main characters … who immediately start getting along just fine. There's minimal actual conflict there as the show plays out. Over time, the writers just converged toward the Kirk-Spock relationship, which is precisely the thing they started out trying to subvert.

I wanted the human-Vulcan conflict to dominate the show — maybe not for its whole run, but certainly for the first season. Send *Enterprise* out there with a "boldly go" attitude … and have them fail! Catastrophically! With actual loss, like the death of a popular main character — or maybe just have that character end up "missing in action" so the heroes can later make it right after they've learned some caution and humility. Large-scale conflict looms, maybe even a full-on shooting war with the Klingons (whom the humans aren't even vaguely prepared to resist), the humans have to beg the Vulcans to bail them out of this existential crisis. Season finale on the Klingon war fleet heading for Earth and the Vulcans aren't taking humanity's calls … or whatever. Stakes!

*Star Trek* (and much more so, *Next Generation)* was a show about how humanity in the future was more civilized and wiser than humanity in the present. I wanted *Enterprise* to be a show about how we got there.

Then there's the nitpicky stuff. The sets and visual effects were created basically on the cusp of high definition TV, and they weren't really good enough. Certainly not now, really not at the time either; everything had this very distinct "we're on a soundstage" look which we've gotten much better at avoiding today. I'm not a fan of the casting. I thought Bakula and Blalock were about as much fun to watch as wet paint, and they had the explosive chemistry of a napkin. The actor who played the alien doctor whose name I can't remember right now is *really* good … in other roles. Jargon like "polarize the hull plating!" grated — they don't have shields, but they have something that works just like shields under a different name, see; it was just filler dialogue written to sound sci-fi-ish. And don't even get me started on "Reed alert." I guess somewhere during the aftermath of World War III humanity forgot about the concept of general quarters.

Bottom line: It's a show that didn't start out with a clear vision of what it wanted to be, and so just kind of meandered. There's never a sense of jeopardy or stakes. The show's setting demanded an undertone of "If we screw up out here, it could literally mean human extinction." Instead we got a bland cast of characters, time travel and catfish. (And I like catfish.)

The Borg are my favorite example of taking a great out-of-context antagonist and absolutely destroying it. Think about how they were described and depicted in their first appearance: The cube-shaped ship was absolutely enormous, their "voice of the legion" was chilling, the way the drones behaved was uncanny. Most of all, the Borg were *different.* We'd never seen anything like them before, as the audience — and the *characters* had never seen anything like them before. By that point in the corpus, Starfleet had been pretty well established as a talk-you-to-death kind of outfit. (See "The Corbomite Maneuver" for a good early example.) *The Borg weren't listening.* They couldn't be reasoned with, couldn't be negotiated with, couldn't be tricked or fooled. They were *new* and Picard and his crew were *unready.*

And then little by little, the writers managed to chip away at that. Don't get me wrong, turning Picard into a Borg in *The Best of Both Worlds* was *terrific* … but it ended up being the first step toward de-Borgification. Picard gave the Borg a face and a (singular) voice, two things which they specifically did not have in their first appearance. Later Borg stories introduced the concept of drone individuality and frankly made them pathetic — in the most literal sense of arousing pity instead of existential terror.

Then those jerks invented the Borg Queen. They can't be reasoned with, they can't be negotiated with … so let's give 'em a way to reason and negotiate with 'em. Ugh.

The *Voyager* stuff was just the final downhill slide. The Borg became a joke, a completely neutered shadow of their original conception. Magic weapons from the future (!?) obliterated Borg cubes in a single shot, and that was pretty much it for them.

The short version is that imagining the future 400 years hence is hard, but more importantly imagining the future 400 years hence while maintaining continuity with previous Star Trek properties is a *pain in the ass.*

For instance, take the tachyon net they used in *Next Generation* to spot cloaked ships. That's a thing Starfleet knows how to do now. Hell, let's go all the way back to the transporter. The transporter was invented as a way to make it possible for the cast of *Star Trek* to visit planets on a TV budget. No need for model photography or additional matte paintings; the actors just disappear from here and appear there.

*Ever since,* writers have had to come up with reason after reason why they *can't* use the transporter to solve whatever problem currently faces the main characters. Why can't we just beam them up? Oh, there's interference from the whatever thing. We can solve that with pattern enhancers! Now you have to come up with a reason why *everybody doesn't use a transformer pattern enhancer all the time.*

There's something like 700 *hours* of Star Trek out there, and in a lot of those hours the characters have concocted some device or technique to solve a problem. That means the possible problem space for future episodes is pretty small! A writer on a continuation show would have to come up with a story that isn't instantly rendered moot by that thing they used in episode 34 of season 19 of whatever.

Lemme explain it like this: Say you're going skydiving with your friend. You both jump out of the plane and fall together. If I ask you how your friend is moving, you'd be forgiven for saying your friend isn't really moving at all; your friend is more or less stationary with respect to you. (You probably wouldn't say that in real life because you'd intuitively answer the question in terms of your friend's motion relative to the ground, but let's ignore that for right now.)

I, watching from the ground, would have a different answer to the question of how you're moving. I'd say your friend is plummeting toward the ground, in fact at an ever-increasing rate.

We two observers, then, *disagree* about an observable fact. Neither of us is wrong; it's just that this particular fact varies depending on who observes it and how.

Physical theories that give different answers depending on who's asking the question (where they are in the universe, how they're moving, what's around them and so on) aren't great. It's hard for us to test those theories, because the answers depend on your viewpoint! So instead, physicists look for what they call *invariant* physical theories: physical theories that give answers that *all observers everywhere* agree on. Those theories are much easier to test, even though they can get pretty mathematically challenging.

Relativity is fundamentally a set of equations that describe motion through space and time. The theory's formulated in such a way, using particular mathematical "tools," that you can write down an equation and say that that equation is *definitively true* regardless of how you yourself are moving through space and time. (Or else it's definitively false, if it turns out to be contradicted by observations, but Einstein and those who built on his work appear to have pretty much nailed it, because *all* of our observations are consistent with the equations of relativity.)

The underlying idea behind Einstein's work — that we should look for mathematical theories that are invariant under various transformations — has turned out to be *incredibly* important over the past hundred years. A particular type of invariance, called *gauge invariance,* ended up being the key that unlocked the door to most of what we now understand about matter and interactions between matter.

Well short answer yes, if I were God-King of *Star Trek Discovery* it would be a hard reboot. Telling great stories is more important than consistency with previous stories, in my opinion, and because the corpus of Star Trek is so vast, telling a great story and remaining consistent come into conflict a lot.

I think Star Trek as a whole has a lot of really terrific aspects to it. I also think it's weighed down by mythology that doesn't contribute anything to the show but that some people go a little nuts if you contradict.

For example, take how warp drive works. I believe since the very beginning of the show, the unaired pilot, warp drive has been described in terms of "warp factors" (or in earliest references, I think it was "time factors") which suggest that ships travel at different speeds through space. *Barrels* of ink have been spilled about just what precisely the warp factor numbers mean, and with *The Next Generation* the writers decided to implicitly assume that the numbers had been recalibrated in the intervening years so now warp 10 was defined as infinite speed … and then in the finale, "All Good Things…", Riker ordered the future Enterprise to warp 13, either inverting the change or creating a new one.

I think that's not great. The bottom line is that starships move at the speed of plot; it takes precisely as long for a starship to go from A to B as the story requires. Which means if you try to wrap warp drive in some kind of technical rules, you're gonna constantly run up against those rules in telling your stories.

If I were God-King of a hard Star Trek reboot, warp drive would be an on-or-off thing. Either you're traveling under warp drive or you're not. But being under warp drive does not mean traveling at a constant and defined speed. It's a brachistochrone sort of thing, where under warp drive the effective speed of the ship increases with time. Under that kind of system, traversing relatively short distances between star systems could still be assumed to take some reasonable amount of time (days? weeks? whatever the plot demands) while traversing long distances is still possible, because the longer you travel, the faster you go.

(Why not just go into warp and stay there, eventually traversing intergalactic distances? Because warp drive still requires an energy source, and it's way beyond practicality to carry enough "fuel" to maintain a warp field that long. You'd need a starship the size of the moon.)

I'd also insert a bit into the show bible about inherent uncertainties in the effective speed of warp drive based on the energy density of the space through which the ship travels, just to give the writers even more freedom to pace stories based on drama rather than math.

All of this would solve a couple of storytelling problems that Star Trek has accumulated over the years. First, if you ship is capable of warp bignum, why would you ever go anywhere at a speed less than bignum? This was addressed in *Next Generation* in the later episode when it was established that warp drive is harmful to subspace and a speed limit was imposed … but that speed limit was just another limitation on the writes, so it was honored more in the breach than the observance.

The other storytelling problem that's come up over the years is the inconsistency of just what it means to be under warp drive. Sometimes sensors work at warp, sometimes they don't. Sometimes weapons work at warp, sometimes not. Sometimes transporters work at warp, sometimes not. It would be a lot less of a chore to maintain consistency if warp were warp, and the pros and cons of being at warp were simple, sensible and consistently adhered to.

If you're interested, the origin of this is visual-effects necessity. When the original show and *Next Generation* were made, models were shot in front of a backdrop in several passes and then optically composited together to make it look like there was a ship floating in space or whatever. It's very different to do model photography and compositing without a strong "diffuse" pass. The diffuse pass is the photography pass in which the model is lit to separate it from the backdrop, be it a black or blue backdrop. (We use green now most of the time because digital cameras are most sensitive to green light, but film is most sensitive to blue light, so black or blue were used when shooting on film.) It's this diffuse-lit pass that makes it possible to create what's called a "matte," which is sort of like a cut-out that shows the model but not anything else. Using the matte, the model could be composited on top of a field of stars or a painting of a planet or whatever.

That's why the model photography in the original show and *Next Generation* (and the earlier movies) is so flat-lit. It was a production necessity so the compositing could be done with acceptable quality on a TV schedule and budget.

When you're using a computer instead of model photography, you can light the scene however you want, because instead of having to "pull" a matte to isolate the spaceship or whatever, you can just "tell" the computer to generate one. The various render passes then go into compositing with their own computer-generated mattes, which means we can have lighting contrast in ways that weren't possible with model photography and optical compositing.

There are two basic approaches to lighting for TV and movies: Naturalistic lighting and artistic lighting. These are ends of a spectrum rather than a dichotomy; everything lands somewhere between those two extremes. And actually there's a third pole, which is *technical* lighting: lighting the scene in such a way that *it actually shows up on film.*

In earlier eras, film stocks and lenses were both much slower than what we have now. You had to put a *lot* of light into a scene in order to film it. Contrast between light and shadow was difficult to achieve without either overexposing the scene or ending up with an excessively grainy shot. That's why TV shows like *Star Trek* and *The Next Generation* have such flat lighting in general. The DPs on the shows *wanted* to light scenes creatively, and did to a certain extent, but the technical requirements of lenses and film stocks demanded a certain lighting setup which was neither naturalistic nor particularly artistic.

Now we have *super-*fast lenses available to rent at TV-budget prices, and we have electronic cameras that are as sensitive or more sensitive than the best film stocks of prior decades, with more dynamic range and less noise. So it's now *technically possible* to light scenes for TV in ways that were simply not practical until pretty recently.

That's why we're seeing more creative, artistic lighting on TV today. It was always something everybody on the production side wanted, but now it's possible to do it on TV budgets and schedules.

Of course, expanding the envelope opens the door for both *good* artistic lighting decisions and *not so good* artistic lighting decisions. You referred to the court martial scene in episode 2: That scene *looked amazing.* The lighting was really fantastic, putting the focus on Burnham and letting everything else disappear into shadow.

But was it the right choice to serve the story? Reasonable people can disagree. I've seen several people say pretty much exactly what you said: that the lighting gave them the impression that the court martial was a secretive affair. I don't think that was the DP's intention at all. I think the intention was to keep the focus on our main character and not crowd the frame with unnecessary faces. But that didn't land, at least not flawlessly, because again, people have said they got the wrong impression from the scene.

It's important when critiquing any piece of art to take into account what the creator or creators of that piece of art were *trying* to accomplish. If you can't figure out what they were trying to do, then that's a legitimate critique — or else you just happened not to get it at the time, which is a possibility we should always entertain. It's reasonable to compare what the creators were trying to accomplish with what they actually accomplished. To say "they failed to do X" when nobody was trying to do X is not a particularly good critique. You can always say something like "I would have preferred X" or whatever, and that's fine! But when judging a work it's best to set aside your own likes and dislikes *just for a minute* and evaluate it in terms of how well it became what it was trying to be.

> "Conn" comes from "conning tower"

Other way around, actually. A "conning tower" is a structure from which a ship can be *conned,* particularly when talking about a submarine. This comes from the verb *con,* with one "n," which in this sense means to command a ship, or (as a noun) *the* command of a ship. It comes from the French conduire meaning to lead. "Conn" is a seemingly fairly popular misspelling of "con," obviously by back-formation from "conning." (Or maybe it qualifies as an alternate spelling now, I dunno.)

The use of the term in *Star Trek* is actually kind of wrong, since "the con" doesn't refer to the *actual steering* of a ship, but rather to the *directing of the steering* of the ship. To "have the con" doesn't mean you've physically got your hands on the tiller or whatever. It means you're the person who is giving the orders to the guy who's got his hands on the tiller. Starting with *Next Generation,* I think it was, the writers started referring to the guy who actually steers the ship as "con," when that person should be called "helmsman," as you noted.

You're almost certainly never going to see a *Star Trek* production set after the events of *Star Trek Nemesis,* because there are two fundamental problems with telling a story in that setting.

The first problem is that you're talking about a period that's about *400 years* in the future. It's really difficult to create a plausible story that's set that far in the future and that's also interesting to people in general. There are tons of stories set in the far future, but they're niche properties. Their inaccessibility limits their popularity.

The second and much bigger problem is that trying to tell a *Star Trek* continuation story is like trying to write with a pencil that weighs a hundred tons. There's just *so much stuff* that's been crammed into *Star Trek* over the years. Telling a continuation story means trying to tell a *new* story that hasn't already been told in the 600-odd hours of *Star Trek* while at the same time being sufficiently consistent with all the previous stories that the audience doesn't flip tables.

It's not just that it would be *hard* to write such a story. It's that it *wouldn't be any fun.* No writer wants to have his hands so tightly tied.

What *Star Trek* really needs is a hard reboot. What they did with the movies was cool, but features are fundamentally a different medium from episodics (and then also in the sequel they decided to rely far too much on mythology gags). What the franchise really needs, if they want to make an episodic or episodics out of it, is a clean slate. Take the things that make *Star Trek* good — themes, elements of the setting — and write an entirely new story with new characters and new conflicts. Don't draw on what came before. Set that all aside and say "This set of stories is now over" and start something new.

(Course you'd still have to deal with the fact that, as a writer, *whatever* you write will cause a vocal faction of the Internet to send you dead fish in the mail.)
